newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 17.

text.p: Prepared by The Broadcast Monitoring Company for Reuters
-- JOBLESS FALL FUELS INFLATION FEAR

Unemployment in the UK fell last month to its lowest level for five and a half years, to a total of 2,073,100, according to the Office for National Statistics. The figures show the largest monthly fall in the jobless rate for almost two years, and have fuelled fears that strong economic growth is stoking up inflationary pressure.
-- SACKED BET CHIEF WINS 3M STG FOR UNFAIR DISMISSAL

A 3 million stg compensation payment to a sacked chief executive has been branded as "disgraceful" by the PIRC, the corporate governance consultancy. The award, to John Clark, former chief executive of BET, was granted for unfair dismissal after a High Court battle involving BET's new owners, Rentokil Initial RTOL. Anne Simpson, joint managing director of PIRC, said the award demonstrated the need for a review of the practice of employing directors on three-year rolling contracts.
-- FRANCE'S LAGARDERE WINS BID BATTLE FOR THOMSON

The French government has chosen Lagardere group ahead of rival bidders Alcatel Alsthom to buy the troubled Thomson defence and electronics group, which it is privatising. Lagardere group was chosen because of the industrial strategy it proposed; it will merge the Thomson-CSF defence subsidiary with its own Matra defence and high technology business to create Europe's largest defence electronics company, and will sell the Thomson Multimedia consumer electronics division to Daewoo of South Korea.
-- FORD TO OVERHAUL EUROPEAN ARM AFTER RISE IN LOSSES

Ford Motor Co has reported a loss of $472 million (302 million stg) for its European operations in the three months to the end of September. The figures are $152 million more than the same period last year, largely because of intense competition and also what Ford has described as runaway costs. The company is now planning an overhaul of its European operations, a move likely to entail early retirements and a review of its vehicle line-up.
-- DIRECTORS SAY OPTING OUT OF EURO WILL HIT CITY

A survey of 500 European finance directors undertaken by UK property group Healey & Baker has revealed that over 60 per cent of those interviewed believe Frankfurt would replace the City of London as Europe's leading financial centre if Britain stays outside of European monetary union. A majority of the survey also said they believed London would build on its lead over Frankfurt if both the UK and Germany joined Emu.
-- DEPRECIATION PLAN MAY HIT BREWERS' PROFITS

A discussion paper published by the Accounting Standards Board has suggested that companies with operating properties - such as brewers, hoteliers and retailers - should have to depreciate their value. The board suggests that brewers, for instance, should place a 'residual value' on their pubs which is based on its value when purchased, not on an estimate of its value at the end of its life. The ASB plans would cut reported pre-tax profits of brewers and hoteliers by 10 per cent.
-- WICKES REPORT CRITICISES AUDITOR

A report into the case of DIY retailer Wickes overstating its profits by 51 million stg has revealed some evidence of deception on the part of executives within the company's buying department in concealing the real terms on which suppliers made rebate payments. A circular to shareholders, based on the findings of an inquiry into the affair undertaken by accountants Price Waterhouse and solicitors Linklaters & Paines, says that former chairman and chief executive Henry Sweetbaum must accept 'ultimate responsibility' for the affair.
-- US GROUP TO PUBLISH JOURNALS ON INTERNET

US business and educational publisher McGraw-Hill is planning to launch a 'Science Online' range of journals exclusively on the Internet. Trials of up to five journals will begin early next year, with scheduled launches later in the year. The decision to go ahead with the project, which is intended to challenge traditional academic publishers such as Reed Elsevier, comes after the company was satisfied that security and charging methods are now mature enough to be reliable.
-- DAIMLER-BENZ CONSIDERS BROAD RESTRUCTURING

German conglomerate Daimler-Benz is considering a wide-ranging restructuring plan which could see an in-house merger at the companys Mercedes-Benz car and truck unit. The merger option for Mercedes-Benz, which represents about 80 per cent of the company's business volume, is said to be supported by the majority of Daimler's board. A formal decision on the reshuffle, which will cut management layers in order to give top managers more direct control, is expected before the end of the year.
-- DMG SACKS FIVE IN WAKE OF YOUNG AFFAIR

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell has moved to sack the chief executive and three senior colleagues at its Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) subsidiary following the deception case involving MGAM unit trust manager Peter Young. The executives were sacked without compensation for their failure to control Young, who worked in the international division of MAGM's unit trust business.
